name: Fermented rice water (sake lees)

lead: Sake lees is the solid leftover from sake brewing and has long been a Japanese food. It also appears in masks and creams sold for brightening.
Benefits are mainly reported by users; no clinical trials for appearance were found.

paras: Freeze-dried kasu is reported to contain a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract and antioxidants; tyrosinase is involved in melanin production.
Kasu contains alcohol, and sunscreen is advised in the Wikipedia article for users of masks. No safety trials in skin care were found.

lead: Sake lees, known in Japanese as sake kasu, is the white pressed residue left after sake is drawn from fermented rice mash; it typically contains around 8 percent alcohol.[1] It is used in Japanese cooking and, in skin care, in face masks, bath powder and creams marketed for brightening and moisture.[1]

The Wikipedia article attributes claimed skin benefits mostly to user reports and to antioxidants in the masks, and notes that freeze-dried kasu contains an extract that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production.[1] No clinical trials in the sources reviewed tested it for appearance.
infobox: Sake kasu, sake filtrate, rice filtrate ferment

paras: Koji enzymes break rice starch into sugar, yeast converts it to alcohol, and the mash is pressed to extract sake, leaving kasu.[1] It contains protein, carbohydrates, fat, B vitamins, fibre, peptides and amino acids.[1] Kasu is part of Japan's "no waste" food culture.[1]

Homemade masks combine kasu with ingredients such as citrus juice, honey, rice water, aloe vera or rose water.[1] The Wikipedia article cites user reports of brighter, moisturised skin and attributes this to antioxidants in the mask; because of the alcohol content it says sunscreen is recommended.[1] Freeze-dried kasu is described as containing triacylglycerols and a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract, which is why it is considered a possible anti-browning ingredient.[1]
